{{Short description|Projective plane}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Cayley plane''' (or '''octonionic projective plane''') '''P'''<sup>2</sup>('''O''') is a [[projective plane]] over the [[octonion]]s.<ref name="Baez2002">Baez (2002).</ref> 

The Cayley plane was discovered in 1933 by [[Ruth Moufang]], and is named after [[Arthur Cayley]] for his 1845 paper describing the octonions.

== Properties ==
In the Cayley plane, lines and points may be defined in a natural way so that it becomes a 2-dimensional [[projective space]], that is, a [[projective plane]]. It is a [[non-Desarguesian plane]], where  [[Desargues' theorem]] does not hold.

More precisely, as of 2005, there are two objects called Cayley planes, namely the real and the complex Cayley plane.
The '''real Cayley plane''' is the [[symmetric space]] [[F4 (mathematics)|F<sub>4</sub>]]/Spin(9), where F<sub>4</sub> is a compact form of an [[exceptional Lie group]] and Spin(9) is the [[spin group]] of nine-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] (realized in F<sub>4</sub>). It admits a cell decomposition into three cells, of dimensions 0, 8 and 16.<ref name="IlievManivel05">Iliev and Manivel (2005).</ref>

The '''complex Cayley plane''' is a [[homogeneous space]] under the complexification of the group [[E6 (mathematics)|E<sub>6</sub>]] by a [[Borel subgroup|parabolic subgroup]] ''P''<sub>1</sub>. It is the closed orbit in the projectivization of the minimal complex representation of E<sub>6</sub>. The complex Cayley plane consists of two complex F<sub>4</sub>-orbits: the closed orbit is a quotient of the complexified F<sub>4</sub> by a parabolic subgroup, the open orbit is the complexification of the real Cayley plane,<ref name="Ahiezer83">Ahiezer (1983).</ref> retracting to it.
